captions.instagram:
How does a matchstick work?

A match is fire stored in two halves: a head that is hard to light, and the missing key on the side of the box. Strike one in slow motion, follow five steps from a 0.03 joule rub to a burning stick, tilt the flame, and meet the workers who paid for cheap matches.

→ A match is fire stored in two halves: a head on the stick, and the missing key on the box.
→ The head is the lock. The key, red phosphorus, is on the box. Scrape a wall: heat, but no flame.
→ On the strip, a 0.03 joule stroke makes a hot spot near 300 °C. Each step then lights the next.
→ The head burns for one second. A film of wax catches in that time and hands the flame to the wood.
→ Tilt it head-down and the flame climbs the stick about five times faster: hot gas rises.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/matchstickclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a matchstick work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A match is fire stored in two halves: a head that is hard to light, and the missing key on the side of the box. Strike one in slow motion, follow five steps from a 0.03 joule rub to a burning stick, tilt the flame, and meet the workers who paid for cheap matches.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/matchstickclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/matchstickclear

In this video:
• Fire stored in two halves. A safety match is a waxed splint about 43 mm long with a head of oxidiser, a little fuel, powdered glass and glue.
• Lock and key. A 3 cm stroke does only about 0.03 joule of work, but it goes into a patch smaller than a pinhead in a few hundredths of a second.
• The flame takes hold. The head burns for about a second.
• From a log to a box of fifty. A log is peeled into veneer and chopped into splints.
• The human cost, and the fix. Early matches used white phosphorus, which lights at about 30 °C and gave workers phossy jaw.
• Before and after the match. A fire drill makes an ember at about 400 °C with a dozen watts of rubbing.
